summary: Specifies Neda's Efficient Mail Submission and Delivery (EMSD) protocol, version 1.3, which focuses narrowly on submitting and delivering short mail messages with a clear emphasis on efficiency. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a streamlined way to send very short messages, with fewer back-and-forth steps than regular email, so it is quick on small devices.

subtitle: Efficient mail submission and delivery for wireless and bandwidth-limited networks.

tldr.problem: Existing email protocols like SMTP are inefficient for wireless networks and devices with severe bandwidth constraints, requiring many round-trips and large message sizes. Mobile devices and pagers need a more lightweight way to send and receive short messages.
tldr.mechanism: EMSD builds on reliable connectionless remote operations (ESRO) over UDP to minimize packet count and message size. It uses binary encoding, simplified operations, and point-to-point transfer focusing only on submission and delivery between a user agent and a server agent.
tldr.outcome: EMSD can be 3 to 5 times more efficient than SMTP for short messages in wireless networks. It is intended primarily for IP-based two-way paging and as an adjunct to existing mail protocols, not as a replacement for SMTP.

facts.label: Efficiency gain over SMTP
facts.value: 3 to 5 times fewer packets and bytes for short messages

facts.label: Transport protocol
facts.value: ESRO (Efficient Short Remote Operations) over UDP

today: RFC 2524 is an Informational RFC documenting a protocol used primarily in private wireless IP networks and IP-based two-way paging systems. It has not been obsoleted but is intended for narrow use cases and not recommended for general Internet deployment due to security and congestion control limitations.

sections.title: Internet Mail and the Need for Efficiency
sections.content:
Email on the Internet has grown organically over decades. Protocols like SMTP were designed for simplicity and compatibility with legacy systems, not efficiency. Modern mobile devices and wireless networks have changed the requirements: users want to send short messages quickly from phones and pagers over links that charge by the byte or suffer from high latency.

The split between mail user agents (on client devices) and servers has become common, with users fetching mail via POP or IMAP. This model works but pulls messages on demand rather than delivering them actively when they arrive. EMSD addresses both problems: it submits and delivers short messages with minimal overhead and supports a push model where the server actively notifies the client of new mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular email was invented when everyone was connected to big computers in offices. Now people use phones and pagers that are slow and expensive to connect, so we need a faster way to send short messages.

sections.title: The EMSD Protocol Design
sections.content:
EMSD defines two independent components: the EMSD Format Standard (EMSD-FS) for encoding messages, and the EMSD Protocol (EMSD-P) for transfer. The format uses binary encoding (ASN.1 with Basic Encoding Rules) rather than text, which saves bytes. The protocol layers on top of Efficient Short Remote Operations (ESRO), which provides reliable, connectionless remote procedure calls over UDP.

The protocol distinguishes between submission (user agent pushing a message to a server agent) and delivery (server agent pushing a message to a user agent). Each direction uses a minimal set of operations: submit and deliveryControl for submission, deliver and submissionControl for delivery. Supporting operations allow verification of receipt and control of message segmentation when a message is larger than can fit in one packet.

EMSD uses UDP port 642 (named esro-emsdp) and ESRO's 2-way or 3-way handshake to guarantee reliable delivery without maintaining a connection state.
sections.plainLanguage: EMSD has a special binary format for messages that takes up less space than regular email text. It talks over simple, quick exchanges rather than opening a long connection.

sections.title: Message Format and Information Objects
sections.content:
EMSD messages are encoded in binary using ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules with strict restrictions to minimize size. Definite-length encoding is required, the short form is used when possible, and strings are never constructed (split across multiple chunks).

An EMSD message includes headers (source port, destination, sender and recipient addresses, timestamps) and a body part. The body can be plain ASCII text or other content types. Messages support optional security elements for authentication and can be split across multiple segments if needed, with reassembly on the receiving end.

The protocol defines a message identifier for deduplication, so if a submission or delivery message is retransmitted due to a timeout, the receiving server will recognize it and not double-process it. It also specifies an ProtocolVersionNumber field to allow future revisions to coexist.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are packed tight like compressed files instead of using readable text. They have sender and recipient addresses, timestamps, and can be cut into pieces if they are too big to fit in one packet.

sections.title: Submission and Delivery Procedures
sections.content:
When a user agent wants to submit a message, it sends a submit operation to the server agent with the message content and recipient information. The server responds immediately, either accepting the message or rejecting it. The user agent can invoke deliveryControl later to check on delivery status or request notifications when the message reaches the recipient.

When the server has a message to deliver to a user agent, it sends a deliver operation. The user agent can verify receipt by invoking deliveryVerify in return, or the server can invoke submissionControl to check on the user's ability to receive messages. If a user agent goes offline, the server stores the message and retries delivery when the agent comes back online.

The entire exchange can complete in as few as two round-trip packets in the common case: one for submission (user to server) and one for acknowledgement (server to user). Queries and notifications add additional exchanges only when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The user's phone sends a message to the server, which says 'got it'. If the phone later wants to know if the message arrived, it can ask. The server can also push messages to the phone when new mail arrives.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The IESG notes in the RFC that EMSD has limited security: passwords are sent in clear text. For wireless networks, implementors must provide encryption at the link layer to protect credentials. The protocol is suitable only for private networks or for use behind a gateway that filters EMSD traffic to and from the public Internet, where an EMSD-to-SMTP gateway sits between the wireless network and the wider Internet.

EMSD also lacks provisions for non-ASCII text and has no built-in congestion control, making it unsuitable for general Internet use. The RFC includes rationale for design choices: using ESRO instead of TCP saves overhead, using ASN.1 and binary encoding minimizes size, and the RPC model keeps the state machine simple.

The protocol is extensible through optional parameters and future versions, allowing new features to be added without breaking older implementations. Implementations must support reliable deduplication of retransmitted operations.
sections.plainLanguage: EMSD sends passwords without hiding them, so it needs encryption in the network itself. It works best in private wireless networks or when messages are converted to regular email before leaving the wireless bubble.
